q: Nina builds picture frames. The first rectangular frame she builds has a perimeter of 26 inches. The length of one of the sides is shown. For her next frame, she keeps the shorter side the same length. The longer side is longer than the shorter side by 2 times the length of the shorter side. What is the perimeter of the next frame?
key: Answer: D. Two sides of 8 use 16 inches, so the other two sides share 26 − 16 = 10, and each is 5. So 8 is the longer side and 5 is the shorter side. In the next frame the shorter side stays 5. The longer side is 5 PLUS 2 × 5 more: 5 + 10 = 15, which is 3 times the shorter side. Perimeter: 2 × (5 + 15) = 40. C makes the longer side only 2 times the shorter side (10), missing the "longer than ... by" part. A is the new longer side. B is one length plus one width.
ref: Tier: Hard · Topic: Perimeter · Follows QR9 #1 (parent review 11/4) · New problem

topic: Comparing Adding Subtracting Bar Graph Data Table Values
q: The table shows the number of miles five friends ran each month. How many more miles did Rosa run than Tess in March, June, and August combined?
key: Answer: B. Rosa: 14 + 18 + 23 = 55. Tess: 17 + 11 + 19 = 47. 55 − 47 = 8. Month by month works too, but watch March: Tess ran MORE (17 vs 14), so March counts as −3: −3 + 7 + 4 = 8. D adds 3 + 7 + 4, treating March as if Rosa ran more. A reads April instead of August (her Lower 5 mix-up). C reads July instead of June.
ref: Tier: Hard · Topic: Comparing Adding Subtracting Bar Graph Data Table Values · Follows QR9 #3 (parent review 11/4) · New problem

q: Each shape shown represents a different digit from 1 through 9. What is the value of ○?
key: Answer: D. The hundreds digit of the answer is 5, but △ + something carried could make 5, so start with the ones column: ○ + △ ends in 1, so ○ + △ = 11 and 1 carries. Tens column: ○ + △ + 1 = 12, so 2 is written and 1 carries. Hundreds: △ + 1 = 5, so △ = 4 and ○ = 11 − 4 = 7. Check: 477 + 44 = 521. C forgets the carry (△ = 5). B is △. A does not work: ○ = 8 would need △ = 3 (8 + 3 = 11), and 388 + 33 = 421, not 521.
ref: Tier: Hard · Topic: Cryptarithm / digit substitution · Follows QR9 #5 (parent review 11/4) · New problem

q: How many numbers between 67 and 85 are divisible by 4?
key: Answer: C. List them: 68, 72, 76, 80, 84, so 5. The shortcut (85 − 67) ÷ 4 = 4.5 → 4 is wrong; write the first and last multiple, then count.
ref: Tier: Hard · Topic: Counting Multiples within a Range · Built on her real-test miss: Lower 5 MA #29; QR9 #36 · Real item used verbatim (gid 978)

q:
○ + ○ + △ = 22
○ + △ + △ = 20
What is the value of △?
key: Answer: B. Add the two lines: three ○ and three △ make 42, so ○ + △ = 14. The second line is (○ + △) + △ = 20, so 14 + △ = 20 and △ = 6. Check the first line: 8 + 8 + 6 = 22. A is ○ − △. C is ○. D is ○ + △ (one step early).
ref: Tier: Hard · Topic: Algebra with Geometric Shapes · Follows QR9 #9 (parent review 11/4) · New problem

topic: Area and Perimeter of Complex Polygons
q: The figure is made from eight identical squares. The perimeter of the figure is 36 centimeters. What is the area of the figure?
key: Answer: B. Go around the outside and count the square sides: there are 18. 36 ÷ 18 = 2, so each square is 2 by 2 with area 4. Eight squares: 8 × 4 = 32. Mark each side with a tick as you count it. On QR9 #10 she counted 11 sides where there were 10.
ref: Tier: Hard · Topic: Area and Perimeter of Complex Polygons · Follows QR9 #10 (parent review 11/4) · Real item used verbatim (gid 1060)

q: Leo practiced piano for 2 13 hours on Saturday and 1 34 hours on Sunday. How many minutes did Leo practice in all? (1 hour = 60 minutes)
key: Answer: C. Change each part to minutes first: 2 hours = 120, 1/3 hour = 20, so 140. 1 hour = 60, 3/4 hour = 45, so 105. 140 + 105 = 245. No fraction adding needed. D uses 1/3 hour = 30. A uses 3/4 hour = 15.
ref: Tier: Hard · Topic: Multi-step unit conversion (off-by-10, multi-step) · Follows QR9 #12 (parent review 11/4) · New problem

q: Which expression is equal to 8 × (6 + 3) − 4?
key: Answer: D. The 8 multiplies BOTH numbers in the parentheses: (8 × 6) + (8 × 3). The − 4 is outside, so it stays. Check: 8 × 9 − 4 = 68 and 48 + 24 − 4 = 68. B drops the − 4.
ref: Tier: Hard · Topic: Order of Operations and Equivalence · Built on her real-test miss: Lower 2 MA #26 · Real item used verbatim (ma_library: ORDER OF OPERATIONS & EQUIVALENCE #3)

q: A ribbon is 3.2 meters long. Kim cuts off 34 meter and then 1.15 meters. How many meters of ribbon are left?
key: Answer: A. 3/4 = 0.75. 3.2 − 0.75 = 2.45, and 2.45 − 1.15 = 1.3. Line up the decimal points (3.20). B reads 3/4 as 0.34. C forgets the 3/4 cut. D stops after the first cut.
ref: Tier: Hard · Topic: Converting to a Decimal · Follows QR9 #13 (parent review 11/4) · New problem

topic: Divisibility / number constraints (Serena/Who am I style)
q: Sally chooses a number at random from a hat containing integers from 10 - 20. The number is prime. When this number is subtracted from 20, the result is also prime. The largest number in the hat is divisible by the sum of the chosen number's digits. What is the number that Sally chose?
key: Answer: B. Check each choice against every rule, one at a time, and cross it out as soon as one rule fails. All four are prime. 20 − 11 = 9 and 20 − 19 = 1 are not prime, so 11 and 19 are out. Digit sums: 13 → 4 and 17 → 8. 20 ÷ 4 = 5, but 20 ÷ 8 is not whole, so the answer is 13.
ref: Tier: Hard · Topic: Divisibility / number constraints (Serena/Who am I style) · Follows QR9 #15 (parent review 11/4) · Real item used verbatim (gid 1497)

topic: Divisibility / number constraints (Serena/Who am I style)
q: Ted picks a two-digit prime number where the first digit is less than the second digit. The difference of its digits is also prime and is a factor of the sum of its digits. Both of these results are less than 6. What is the two-digit prime that Ted chose?
key: Answer: B. First digit less than second: 11 (equal) and 31 are out. 13: difference 2 (prime), sum 4, 2 is a factor of 4, both less than 6. 23: difference 1, which is not prime. So 13. Test every rule on every choice that is left.
ref: Tier: Hard · Topic: Divisibility / number constraints (Serena/Who am I style) · Follows QR9 #15 (parent review 11/4) · Real item used verbatim (gid 1501)

topic: Classification of Numbers, given a Set
q: Two different prime numbers are multiplied. What will always describe the product of the two numbers?
key: Answer: A. The product has at least the two primes as factors, so it is always composite. It is NOT always odd: 2 is a prime number, and 2 × 3 = 6 is even. It is not always even either: 3 × 5 = 15.
ref: Tier: Hard · Topic: Classification of Numbers, given a Set · Built on her real-test miss: Lower 2 MA #29 (2 is prime) · New problem

q: The price of a game is increased by 50%. The new price is then decreased by 20%. What is the overall percent increase or percent decrease from the original price?
key: Answer: D. Start with $100. Up 50%: 100 + 50 = 150. Down 20% of 150: 150 − 30 = 120. 120 is 20 more than 100, so it is a 20% increase. B just subtracts the percents (50 − 20). C adds them.
ref: Tier: Hard · Topic: Percent Increase Decrease basic · Follows QR9 #16 (parent review 11/4) · New problem

topic: Total Shaded Area given Figure with Equal Divisions
q: The shaded area on the grid represents the part of a rectangular garden that has been planted. Each small square is the same size. What percentage of the garden has been planted?
key: Answer: C. The grid is 10 squares across and 5 down, so there are 50 squares. 18 are shaded. 18/50 = 36/100 = 36%. A reads the count as the percent. D counts only 8 columns (18/40). Count the rows and columns of the whole grid first, then the shaded squares, writing each number down.
ref: Tier: Hard · Topic: Total Shaded Area given Figure with Equal Divisions · Follows QR9 #17 (parent review 11/4) · New problem

q: Ava had □ stickers and then she gave ○ of them to Ben. Now, Ben has △ more stickers than Ava had. Which expression represents the number of stickers Ben had to begin with?
key: Answer: A. Ava HAD □. Ben now has △ more than that: □ + △. Before Ava gave him ○, he had ○ fewer: □ + △ − ○. Try numbers: □ = 10, ○ = 3, △ = 5. Ben now has 15, so he started with 12. Only A gives 12.
ref: Tier: Hard · Topic: Translating Math Expressions · Follows QR9 #19 (parent review 11/4) · New problem

q: Students were asked to write a new number using all the rules shown. What digit is in the hundreds place of the new number?
key: Answer: B. Odd means it ends in 3 or 9. To be as small as possible, the first digit should be the smallest digit that is not 0, which is 3, so it ends in 9: 3 _ _ _ 9, filled smallest first: 30,469. The hundreds digit is 4. A number cannot start with 0. Write the whole number down before reading the place.
ref: Tier: Hard · Topic: Value of Digits · Built on her real-test miss: Lower 3 #31; QR9 #24 · New problem
diagram:
RULES FOR THE NEW NUMBER
1. The number must have 5 digits.
2. It must use each of the digits 0, 3, 4, 6, and 9 one time.
3. The number must be odd.
4. The number must be as small as possible.

q: Tabitha has □ buttons. She first gives away ○ buttons, and then she sorts the remaining buttons into ◇ containers. Which expression can be used to determine the number of buttons in each container?
key: Answer: A. Start with □, give away ○: □ − ○ are left. Sort those into ◇ containers: (□ − ○) ÷ ◇. The parentheses make the giving away happen first.
ref: Tier: Hard · Topic: Translating Math Expressions · Follows QR9 #19 (parent review 11/4) · Real item used verbatim (gid 1054)

topic: Nth Term, given Arithmetic Sequence, Progressive Pattern, etc.
q: In a sequence, each number is 7 more than the number before it. The 9th number in the sequence is 65. What is the 25th number in the sequence?
key: Answer: D. From the 9th to the 25th number is 25 − 9 = 16 steps. 16 × 7 = 112, and 65 + 112 = 177. A is 16 × 7, one step early: it still needs adding to 65. B uses 15 steps. C is 25 × 7.
ref: Tier: Hard · Topic: Nth Term, given Arithmetic Sequence, Progressive Pattern, etc. · Follows QR9 #26 (parent review 11/4) · New problem

q: Four students ran on the same track. Kai ran 34 of a mile, Lila ran 0.7 of a mile, Max ran 58 of a mile, and Nia ran 72% of a mile. Which list shows the students in order from the longest run to the shortest?
key: Answer: A. Write each as a decimal next to the name: Kai 0.75, Lila 0.70, Max 0.625, Nia 0.72. Longest to shortest: 0.75, 0.72, 0.70, 0.625, which is Kai, Nia, Lila, Max. B is shortest to longest. C puts 0.7 before 0.72.
ref: Tier: Hard · Topic: Comparing & Ordering Fractions & Decimals · Follows QR9 #22 (parent review 11/4) · New problem

q: Two cubes are shown. Cube A has sides 3 centimeters long. Cube B is 4 times as wide as Cube A. How many Cube A's can fit inside Cube B?
key: Answer: B. Cube B is 4 Cube A's wide, 4 long, and 4 tall, so 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 fit. A is 3 × 4 (side times width). C is 4 × 27. D is 64 × 3: the 3 cm side does not matter, only how many times as wide.
ref: Tier: Hard · Topic: Comparing Volume of Cubes · Built on her real-test miss: Lower 4 #36 (and three other cube misses) · New problem

q: The length of AD is 15. The length of AB is x. The length of CD is y. What is the length of BC?
key: Answer: D. BC is what is left of AD after taking away AB and CD: 15 − x − y. Taking away x and then y is the same as taking away (x + y), so 15 − (x + y). A is the parentheses removed wrong: a minus sign in front of the parentheses changes the sign of EVERYTHING inside, so −(x + y) = −x − y, not −x + y.
ref: Tier: Hard · Topic: Split Line Segments · Follows QR9 #27 (parent review 11/4) · New problem

topic: Finding Area/Perimeter of Rectangle, given Length & Width
q: If the perimeter of a square is increased from 12 centimeters to 16 centimeters, then by what amount will its area increase?
key: Answer: C. Perimeter 12 means a side of 3, area 9. Perimeter 16 means a side of 4, area 16. The area grows by 16 − 9 = 7. A is the change in perimeter, not area.
ref: Tier: Hard · Topic: Finding Area/Perimeter of Rectangle, given Length & Width · Follows QR9 #35 (parent review 11/4) · Real item used verbatim (gid 1061)

q: The length of AC is x. The length of BD is y. The length of AD is 15. What is the length of BC?
key: Answer: A. AC and BD together cover all of AD plus BC a second time, so x + y = 15 + BC and BC = x + y − 15. A is the same thing: x − (15 − y) = x − 15 + y, because the minus in front of the parentheses flips −y to +y. C removes the parentheses without flipping the sign. Check with A = 0, B = 4, C = 9, D = 15: x = 9, y = 11, BC = 5, and A gives 9 − 4 = 5.
ref: Tier: Hard · Topic: Split Line Segments · Follows QR9 #27 (parent review 11/4) · New problem

topic: Remaining Amount after Reducing by Fractions
q: Sam had 12 marbles and 15 shells. He lost 14 of his marbles and 23 of his shells. How many marbles and shells does he have left?
key: Answer: C. Marbles: 1/4 of 12 is 3, so 9 are left. Shells: 2/3 of 15 is 10, so 5 are left. 9 + 5 = 14. B is how many he LOST. A counts only the marbles. D takes 1/3 of the shells instead of 2/3.
ref: Tier: Hard · Topic: Remaining Amount after Reducing by Fractions · Built on her real-test miss: Lower 1 MA #25; QR9 #38 · New problem

topic: Finding Area/Perimeter of Rectangle, given Length & Width
q: The area of a square is 25 feet². The area of another square is 11 feet² more than the first square. What is the perimeter of the second square?
key: Answer: C. The second square has area 25 + 11 = 36, so its side is 6 and its perimeter is 4 × 6 = 24. B is the first square's perimeter.
ref: Tier: Hard · Topic: Finding Area/Perimeter of Rectangle, given Length & Width · Follows QR9 #35 (parent review 11/4) · Real item used verbatim (gid 1062)

q: Max has two equal-sized buckets of sand. The first bucket is n8 full. The second bucket is 13 full. The sand from the first bucket is poured into the second bucket. Which statement best describes the amount of sand once the buckets are combined?

choices.A: If n = 1, then the amount of sand is less than 13 of a bucket.
choices.B: If n = 2, then the amount of sand is less than 12 of a bucket.
choices.C: If n = 5, then the sand will not all fit in 1 bucket.
choices.D: If n = 6, then the sand will not all fit in 1 bucket.

key: Answer: D. Use 24ths: 1/3 = 8/24 and n/8 = 3n/24. n = 1: 11/24, more than 8/24, so A is false (the second bucket alone is already 1/3). n = 2: 14/24, more than 12/24, so B is false. n = 5: 23/24, which still fits, so C is false. n = 6: 26/24, more than 1 bucket, so D is true.
ref: Tier: Hard · Topic: Adding and Subtracting Fractions · Follows QR9 #34 (parent review 11/4) · New problem

q: A survey was done to determine which sport was preferred between soccer, football, and basketball. There were 3 times as many votes for soccer as football and 5 times as many votes for football as for basketball. If there is a total of 42 people in the survey, how many people voted for soccer?
key: Answer: C. Let basketball be 1 part. Football is 5 parts and soccer is 3 × 5 = 15 parts: 1 + 5 + 15 = 21 parts = 42, so 1 part = 2. Soccer = 15 × 2 = 30.
ref: Tier: Hard · Topic: Word Problems with Ratios · Follows QR9 #32 (parent review 11/4) · Real item used verbatim (gid 1136)

q: Wendy can type 60 words in a minute. Wendy needs to type a 1,000-word essay and a 2,000-word short story. Which equation can be used to find t, the total time, in minutes, it will take Wendy to type both the essay and the short story?
key: Answer: D. First the total words: 1,000 + 2,000 = 3,000. She types 60 a minute, so the minutes are 3,000 ÷ 60 = 50. The parentheses make the adding happen first. C multiplies, which would make the time bigger than the words.

q: Which number is divisible by both 3 and 4?
key: Answer: C. 24 ÷ 3 = 8 and 24 ÷ 4 = 6. A number divisible by both 3 and 4 is divisible by 12. That is the reminder for the next problem type.

q: Omar and 14 other students each collected the same number of cans. Which number could be the total number of cans the students collected?
key: Answer: A. Omar and 14 others is 15 students, so the total must divide by 15, which means by 3 AND by 5. 1,245: ends in 5, and 1 + 2 + 4 + 5 = 12 divides by 3. B divides by 14 (forgot Omar). C divides by 5 but not 3. D divides by 3 but not 5.
